title: The Two Trees and the Five Members: Life and Death as Corresponding Structures
arc: The teaching opens with two trees and unfolds each as a five-membered organism: the Beautiful Tree whose members are the five faculties bearing Jesus as fruit and conveying the soul upward through the degrees to the Mind of Truth, and the Bitter Tree whose same five members invert downward into the bolos; it closes by insisting the two trees did not arise from one another but from two distinct origins.
reading:
The whole chapter is built on a single architectural insight: Life and Death are not vague opposites but precisely corresponding structures, each with the same five members, each producing fruit according to its root. The teaching names the two trees at the outset and then walks through each as a living organism, showing how the very same faculties — reflection, counsel, teaching, thought, mind — function in the Beautiful Tree as a ladder of ascent and in the Bitter Tree as a chain of descent.

The Beautiful Tree is read first. Its noetic branches stand upon a body, and its fruits are Jesus the Radiance who is glorious — that is, the works that grow on this tree are Divine Truth itself shining forth as Redeemer. The tree has five members, and these members are not abstract powers but the five intellectual faculties of the soul, each identified with a cosmic person of light. Reflection is the lowest receiving faculty: souls that come up are first received here. From reflection they are conveyed upward to counsel; from counsel upward to teaching, which is the First Man, dwelling in the ship of the night (the moon as receptive vessel of light); from teaching upward to thought, which is the Third Ambassador, dwelling in the ship of the day (the sun as Divine Truth shining); and the great Thought finally gathers them inward to the mind, which is the God of Truth, the great Mind of all the aeons of glory. The whole tree is therefore the Pillar of Glory read as a living organism: a vertical anatomy of regeneration in which each faculty hands the soul up to the next, and each station is the indwelling of a divine person whose ship or seat that faculty is. This is why its fruits are sweet and give life and light forever — every member is in conjunction with the Lord, and the conveyance upward never breaks.

The Bitter Tree is then read against this pattern, member for member, so that the correspondence is exact and inverted. It too has five members — reflection, counsel, teaching, thought, mind — but in it each faculty is the opposite-state of the divine faculty above. Its reflection is the law of death; its counsel is metensomatosis, the corrupt cycling of state through bodies in place of true conveying-upward; its teaching is the furnaces of fire and the gehenna full of smoke, where doctrine has become the burning of self-love and the obscuring confusion of false thought; its thought is a stronghold, falsity confirmed and walled in upon itself; and its mind is the bolos, the final clod, the consummating binding in which all unredeemed darkness is fixed forever. Where the Beautiful Tree's members lift the soul through ship of night and ship of day inward to the Mind of all aeons, the Bitter Tree's members drag everything down through smoke and furnace and stronghold to the final compacted state in which there is no repentance. Its fruits are bitter; it grows in the bitter land of death and darkness, as the Beautiful Tree grows in the beautiful land where there is no death and no darkness.

Hyle is the bitter tree. The closing movement of the teaching insists, with marked emphasis, that these two trees did not come into being from one another and did not come forth from a single man. Their origins are distinct: each rises toward — or sinks toward — its own aeon, the one toward the aeon of light, the other producing its evil fruit only from itself. The point is doctrinal: the structure of correspondence is real on both sides, but the substance is two. The same five-fold form of the natural-rational interface either becomes the upward Pillar through which Jesus the Radiance is borne as fruit, or becomes the downward column terminating in the bolos. What determines which tree a soul belongs to is not the architecture of its faculties — those are common — but the root from which those faculties draw. Souls that fall upon the ground reach one or the other; those who believe are gathered with the Beautiful Tree's fruit, while what springs from the darkness is carried away and bound hidden within the clod forever.

The spiritual process being taught is therefore twofold and exact. Regeneration is the operation of the Beautiful Tree: each faculty in its turn must become the dwelling of a divine person, and each must hand the soul up to the next, so that reflection passes to counsel, counsel to the teaching that is the First Man, teaching to the thought that is the Ambassador, thought inward to the Mind of Truth. Damnation is the operation of the Bitter Tree: the very same faculties, severed from their divine indwellers, become law-of-death, transmigration, gehenna, stronghold, and final clod. The teaching is asking the hearer to recognize that the five members in himself are already arranged either as the ladder of Jesus the Radiance or as the descending chain to the bolos, and that there is no third tree and no shared root between them.
